title: Central banks can move spending today just by promising what rates will be later
body: On 12 October 2026 Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the economics prize in memory of Alfred Nobel, “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”. In 1978 Hall showed that households spend according to what they expect to earn, so their spending changes only when news arrives. Woodford built such forward-looking households, and firms that set prices with the future in mind, into a model that central banks now use around the world. In it, a lower interest rate makes saving pay less, so people spend more now; and because they look ahead, the rates they expect for the coming years count as well as today’s. So a central bank can steer with words, by announcing a path for future rates: **forward guidance**, used in the US while rates sat near zero from 2008 to 2015. It works only if people believe it. On 16 September 2026 the [Federal Reserve raised its rate](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20260916a.htm) to 3.75–4%, its first increase since July 2023, and its next decision is due on 28 October.

slides.question: In a 1982 study by Robert Hall and Frederic Mishkin, what share of households planned spending on expected income?
slides.explanation: About 80%. The rest lived from hand to mouth, spending what came in. Models used by central banks today include both kinds of household.

slides.alt: Animation on banknote green: houses and factories gather into the economy; a spending line that steps only on news; a rate path in brass beside today's spending in mint, which rises most when lower rates are promised for two years; then the Fed's rate since 2022, up to 3.75–4%.

slides.prompt: Keep today’s rate at 3% and lift spending today by 1.5%, with a promise alone.
slides.takeaway: Promise rates 0.75 points lower and, if everyone believes it, spending rises 1.5% at once with no cut today. With less belief you need a bigger promise. That is in this simple model; real effects are weaker.

slides.heading: Why words count
slides.text: In these models, people and firms decide today on their best guess about the future. A central bank that says clearly what it plans changes those guesses, so its words work a little like extra rate decisions. That is why central banks explain their plans so carefully, and why a promise has to be believable.

slides.question: In Woodford’s model, why can a promise about future rates raise spending now?
slides.explanation: Households and firms look ahead. Lower expected rates make saving less attractive over the coming years, so spending rises now, as long as the promise is believed.
